sections.title: What you will learn to say

blocks.text: In this lesson you learn to say what is where: «there's a pharmacy nearby», «there's milk in the fridge», «there's no bell here», «the key is under the mat». The main new phrase is There is — it means «something exists here».

examples.translation: A pharmacy exists here.
You can find some milk here.
You ask if a toilet exists here.
The door has no bell.

examples.en: The key is under the doormat.
examples.translation: The key is below the mat.

blocks.text: To say something is somewhere, start with There is. Don't start with Here is: that is for handing something over. Then comes a and the thing, and the place goes last: There is a pharmacy here.

examples.translation: A pharmacy exists here.
A library is close to here.
A bakery is here.
An office is on the floor above.

examples.en: There is a clinic inside the building.
examples.translation: A clinic is in this building.

blocks.text: There here does not mean «over there». It is just the start of the phrase «something exists». So There is a pharmacy here is fine: there and here don't fight.

sections.title: There are: when there are several

blocks.text: For more than one thing, use are instead of is and add s to the word: There are banks here. As in lesson 3, you don't put a before several things.

examples.translation: More than one bank is here.
More than one museum is close.
More than one bridge is close.
Some quiet streets are here.
More than one park is close.

drill.why: There is more than one museum, so There are.

blocks.text: First say what exists, then say where. Start with There is and the thing, and put the place at the very end: There is a garden behind the building. It's easier: first the news, then the details.

examples.en: There is a garden behind the building.
examples.translation: The garden is at the back of the building.

examples.en: There is a bench near the garden.
examples.translation: A seat is close to the garden.

examples.en: There is a church behind the bank.
examples.translation: The church is at the back of the bank.

examples.en: There is a market near the bridge.
examples.translation: A market is close to the bridge.

examples.en: There is a lake behind the park.
examples.translation: The lake is past the park.

drill.prompt: Tell a friend: there is a lake behind the park.

blocks.text: To ask, swap the first two words: There is → Is there…? There are → Are there…? Short answers: Yes, there is. No, there isn't. Yes, there are. No, there aren't. Don't ask with the normal order: not There is a toilet here?

examples.en: Is there a dentist near here?
examples.translation: You ask if a dentist is close.
You ask if a toilet is here.
One does exist.
None exists.

examples.en: Are there trams near the bank?
examples.translation: You ask if trams run near the bank.
Several exist.
None exist.

sections.title: Milk, bread, butter: you don't count them

blocks.text: Some things you count: one banana, two bananas. Others you don't: milk, bread, butter, sugar. They have no a in front and no s at the end. To say «there is a bit», use some: There is some milk.

examples.translation: You can find milk here.

examples.en: There is some bread near the basket.
examples.translation: Bread is close to the basket.

examples.en: There is some butter near the bowl.
examples.translation: Butter is close to the bowl.
You can find cheese here.
You can find a few berries here.

blocks.text: With things you don't count, always is, never are: There is some milk, even if it feels like «a lot» of milk.
some — when you say that something is there. any — when you ask if there is any at all, or say there is none. Often both are left out in other languages: «Is there soup?» — Is there any soup?

examples.translation: Milk is here.
You ask if soup is here.
You ask if mushrooms are here.
No juice is here.
No carrots are here.

drill.why: You ask if there is any rice at all, so any.

blocks.text: To say something isn't there, add not: There is not → There isn't, There are not → There aren't. For one thing — isn't a. For several — aren't any.

examples.translation: The door has no bell.
No speaker at the door.
No rails to hold.
No steps at all.

examples.en: There isn't a lawn behind the building.
examples.translation: No grass at the back.

drill.question: The door has no bell. How do you say it?
drill.explain: There is one bell, so isn't.

blocks.text: in — inside something: in the sink, in the basement. on — on top, touching the surface: on the worktop, on the windowsill. under — below: under the doormat. Careful: a windowsill is on, not in.

examples.en: The lemon is in the sink.
examples.translation: Inside the sink.

examples.en: The bicycle is in the basement.
examples.translation: Inside the room under the house.

examples.en: The cups are on the worktop.
examples.translation: On top of the kitchen counter.

examples.en: The plant is on the windowsill.
examples.translation: On the shelf under the window.

examples.en: The key is under the doormat.
examples.translation: Below the mat.

fixes.wrong: The plant is in the windowsill.
fixes.right: The plant is on the windowsill.

fixes.wrong: The key is on under the doormat.
fixes.right: The key is under the doormat.

sections.title: next to, between … and, near, behind

blocks.text: next to — right beside. near — close, but not touching. behind — at the back. between … and — in the middle of two things: two things, two words: between the bank and the library. Use and, not a comma.

examples.en: The bench is next to the lamppost.
examples.translation: Right beside the lamppost.

examples.en: The signpost is near the bridge.
examples.translation: Close to the bridge.

examples.en: The ladder is behind the shed.
examples.translation: At the back of the shed.

examples.en: The bus stop is between the bank and the library.
examples.translation: The bank on one side, the library on the other.

fixes.wrong: The bench is next the lamppost.
fixes.right: The bench is next to the lamppost.

fixes.wrong: The bus stop is between the bank, the library.
fixes.right: The bus stop is between the bank and the library.

drill.why: There are two places, and the stop is in the middle: between … and.

blocks.text: There is — when you tell someone that something exists; they don't know about it yet. The … is — when you both know the thing and you say where it is: The lemon is in the sink. First «it exists», then «where it is».

examples.en: There is a car park near the hotel.
examples.translation: News: a car park exists.

examples.en: The barrier is near the gate.
examples.translation: We both know the barrier.

examples.en: There is a storeroom between the kitchen and the hall.
examples.translation: News: a storeroom exists.

examples.en: The coat rack is behind the door.
examples.translation: We both know the coat rack.

fixes.wrong: There is the lemon in the sink.
fixes.right: The lemon is in the sink.

drill.question: Your sister is looking for the lemon you both know about. It is in the sink. What do you say?
drill.optionA: There is a lemon in the sink.
drill.optionB: The lemon is in the sink.
drill.explain: The lemon is known, you say where it is: The lemon is in the sink.

blocks.text: In speech, There is almost always becomes There's: There's a cashpoint near the bank. There are is not shortened. And «not» is shortened as usual: isn't, aren't.

examples.en: There's a cashpoint near the bank.
examples.translation: A cash machine is near the bank.

examples.en: There's a postbox next to the gate.
examples.translation: A post box is by the gate.

examples.en: There's a vending machine in the hall.
examples.translation: A snack machine is in the hall.

blocks.text: A short «yes» is not shortened: Yes, there is, not Yes, there's.

fixes.wrong: The plant is in the windowsill.
fixes.right: The plant is on the windowsill.

fixes.wrong: There is the lemon in the sink.
fixes.right: The lemon is in the sink.

blocks.text: Two checks. Are you telling someone that something exists, or saying where a thing you both know is? «Exists» — There is / There are. «Where» — The … is. Second: one thing, several, or something you don't count?

«It exists» — There is a… / There are… / There is some… «Is there?» — Is there…? Are there any…? «There isn't» — There isn't a… / There aren't any… The place goes last: in, on, under, next to, near, behind, between … and.

examples.translation: A library is close.
You ask if mushrooms are here.
No steps at all.

examples.en: The cups are on the worktop.
examples.translation: On top of the kitchen counter.
